beats.caption: Same mother. Same baby. My baby is here. He is crying. I am exhausted.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: Everyone says to sleep when he sleeps. Apparently that is also when I’m supposed to do everything else.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: Same baby. Same income. Same need for food. Two ways the next five years could go.
beats.speaker: One mother · two paths

beats.caption: “Have you tried WIC?”
beats.speaker: With WIC · a friend

beats.caption: “Is that food stamps?”
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: “No, WIC helps with food for you and your baby.” Thank God she said something. I had no idea.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I know about food stamps. We have Medicaid. WIC never comes up.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

beats.caption: My friend sends me the number. I call WIC to apply. Before the appointment, I need to gather a few things—starting with my ID.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Then my address and Medicaid information. Medicaid establishes income eligibility. It doesn’t enroll me in WIC.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: There’s still an appointment to arrange. A phone appointment can save a trip—but I still need time for the call.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I’m fully breastfeeding. My package includes $52 a month for produce, plus other foods. Okay. That would help.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: In my other life, nobody tells me about the program. I’m buying the same food, but all of it comes out of my own budget.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Let’s step back from one family. Across the country, getting through the door looks very different.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: WIC reaches 79.6% of eligible people in Vermont, 62.4% in New York, and 41.3% in Louisiana.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: The same federal program. A different chance of receiving help. Nationally, 56.1% of eligible people participate.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: Back to the grocery trip. In rural New York, the next store can be a long way away.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: Keene Valley to this store in Lake Placid: 21.5 miles one way. Now add the baby, the bags, and getting home again.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Without WIC, I can choose where to shop. With WIC, I need a store where I can use the benefits.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: For many families, using the card starts with a trip: more than a mile to a WIC store in a city, or more than ten miles in the countryside. Across the country, 40% of low-income families with young children live beyond those distances.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: This is not one grocery budget. It’s quantities of certain foods, plus dollars for produce.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Right food. Wrong size. Back down the aisle.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I put something back. I’m watching what’s left in my account.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I can’t swap the milk allowance for more fruit. And now the baby is crying.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: The card replaced paper checks. It didn’t remove the rules.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I’m stocking up for the next couple of weeks. First, the eggs, fruit, and vegetables.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Peanut butter and milk. I check the sizes before they reach the scanner.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: More fruit for the kitchen. These come out of my produce dollars.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Chicken, pasta, sauce. WIC helps with specific foods; the rest is still on me.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: The white rice isn’t covered either. I decide to pay for it.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: WIC covers $23.97. I pay $40.11. This time, the food is coming home.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Without WIC, the same groceries take $64.08 from my own money.
beats.speaker: Without WIC · Maya

title: On the card. In the kitchen.

beats.caption: Some months I make the trip. The food I bring home helps.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Some months there’s still food on my benefits when they expire. I meant to go back. Then something else happened.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: The amount on the card and the amount in the kitchen aren’t always the same.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: Another month ends. Then another. Suddenly, the next date on the calendar is his first birthday.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: One candle. A whole year of feeding him. And another deadline to keep the help.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: The renewal reminder arrives. The appointment conflicts with work. I put it aside.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Tomorrow, I remember after the office closes. Then I have to check which documents they need.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: I’m not deciding we don’t need the food. I just can’t deal with this today.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: This time, I call before the deadline. I find an appointment I can manage. I renew.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: He’s two. More groceries. Another appointment.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: He’s three. I know the foods that work for us. I still have to keep coming back.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: He’s four. His need for food hasn’t expired with the paperwork.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: I’ve kept coming back. But how many families manage that? Researchers followed children who enrolled in 2013: only 43.5% participated consistently through four and a half years.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: A newer national snapshot shows the same challenge from another angle. WIC reaches 82.3% of eligible infants, but just 26.9% of eligible four-year-olds.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: One month: up to $52 for produce while I’m fully breastfeeding.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Twelve months: up to $624.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Then $26 a month for my child. One year adds $312.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Two child years add $624 to that first year of help.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Three child years add $936.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Four child years, plus my breastfeeding year: up to $1,872 in available produce benefits.
beats.speaker: With WIC · Maya

beats.caption: Those groceries add up. But do they change what children eat? Researchers looked beyond the grocery bill and scored children’s overall diets on a 100-point scale.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: At age three, children who stayed in WIC into their third year scored 3.6 points higher than those who only received it in year one.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: The difference is modest, but it is visible across the overall diet. Continuing WIC was associated with better diet quality.
beats.speaker: A wider view

beats.caption: Now he is five. The same birthday in both paths.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: WIC can make nutritious food more affordable. But a benefit only helps when a family hears about it, enrolls, finds a store, buys the right foods, and manages to keep renewing.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: Make that work easier: connect families directly to WIC when they receive Medicaid or have a baby; offer appointments and renewals that fit working lives; bring authorized stores closer; and make approved foods and checkout rules easier to understand. Help should be easier to start—and easier to keep.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths

beats.caption: Getting help should take less work.
beats.speaker: Maya · both paths
